result: The study developed and validated a Lyso-IP method for rapid isolation of lysosomes from C. elegans. Transgenic strains expressing LMP-1 tagged with 3×HA and RFP were generated, and lysosomes were purified in ~25 minutes. Purified lysosomes retained acidic pH (LysoTracker positive), showed enrichment of lysosomal markers, and lacked markers of other organelles. Proteomic profiling showed good reproducibility and clear separation between Lyso-IP and flow-through samples.
evaluation: Claims C36-C53 collectively demonstrate successful development of the Lyso-IP method. Western blot data (C49-C50, Figure 1D), imaging data (C43, C47-C48, Figures 1B-C), and proteomic quality metrics (C52-C53, Figure 1E) provide converging evidence. The method is well-validated with appropriate controls and reproducible results across biological replicates.

result: The study identified 216 lysosome-enriched proteins from >6000 detected proteins in wild-type C. elegans, with 178 having mammalian homologs. The proteome includes known lysosomal proteins (cathepsins, ARL8, v-ATPase subunits) and reveals differential enrichment of v-ATPase V0 vs V1 domains, suggesting both free and membrane-associated forms exist. The proteome also includes plasma membrane receptors undergoing endocytosis and lysosomal degradation.
evaluation: Claims C54-C71 are well-supported by proteomic data with stringent selection criteria (≥10-fold enrichment in all replicates, >2-fold vs non-tag controls). The detection of known lysosomal proteins validates the approach, while the differential V0/V1 enrichment (C60-C66, Figure 2D) provides novel insight into v-ATPase assembly states. The identification of plasma membrane proteins (C67-C71) is consistent with known endo-lysosomal trafficking.

result: The study generated tissue-specific Lyso-IP strains (hypodermis, muscle, intestine, neurons) and discovered lysosomal proteome heterogeneity across tissues. Among 216 proteins, 85 showed comparable enrichment across tissues, while 122 showed significant tissue-specific differences (p<0.05). Y58A7A.1, a copper transporter, showed hypodermis-specific lysosomal localization, validated by CRISPR knock-in imaging.
evaluation: Claims C39-C78 demonstrate tissue-specific lysosomal heterogeneity with appropriate statistical analysis (p<0.05) and validation. The generation of tissue-specific strains (C39, C72, Figure 3A) and comparative proteomic analysis (C73-C75, Figure 3F) are well-documented. The Y58A7A.1 validation (C76-C77, Figure 3—supplement 1E) provides strong evidence for functional tissue specificity.

result: The study profiled lysosome-enriched proteomes in four long-lived models (lipl-4 Tg, daf-2(lf), isp-1(lf), glp-1(lf)) and found distinct protein composition changes. The lipl-4 Tg showed the largest change (61% unique proteins, 39% overlap with WT), while other models showed 57-78.5% overlap with WT. Only one protein was shared among all four long-lived strains but absent from WT, suggesting distinct longevity mechanisms influence lysosomal composition differently.
evaluation: Claims C79-C99 are supported by comprehensive proteomic comparisons across multiple longevity models with good reproducibility (Figure 4—supplement 1A-D). The quantitative overlap analysis (C80-C98) and statistical comparisons provide clear evidence for differential lysosomal remodeling. The conclusion that lipl-4 Tg causes larger changes (C99) is well-supported by the overlap percentages.

result: The study discovered specific lysosomal recruitment of AMPK (AAK-2) in lipl-4 Tg worms but not in other longevity models. AAK-2 showed >10-fold enrichment in lipl-4 Tg Lyso-IP but was only detected in WT flow-through. AMPK inactivation reduced lipl-4 Tg lifespan by 29% and suppressed lifespan extension from 72% to 48%, demonstrating AMPK is partially required for lipl-4-induced longevity.
evaluation: Claims C100-C111 are well-supported by proteomic data (C104-C107, Figure 5B) and functional validation through lifespan assays (C109-C110, Figure 5C). The specificity of AMPK recruitment to lipl-4 Tg lysosomes (C108) is demonstrated by its absence in other longevity models. The partial suppression of longevity (C110-C111) indicates AMPK is necessary but not sufficient, which is appropriately interpreted.

result: The lipl-4 Tg worms showed increased enrichment of lysosomal v-ATPase (especially V0 subunits VHA-1,2,3, V1 subunits VHA-11,15, and accessory proteins VHA-19,20), 13 lysosomal channels/transporters, and 16 lysosomal hydrolases compared to WT. These changes were specific to lipl-4 Tg and not observed in daf-2(lf), isp-1(lf), or glp-1(lf) mutants, suggesting increased proportion of mature acidic lysosomes in lipl-4 Tg worms.
evaluation: Claims C115-C118 are supported by proteomic data (Figure 5A) showing specific enrichment patterns in lipl-4 Tg. The conclusion about increased mature lysosomes (C118) is a reasonable inference from the coordinated enrichment of acidification machinery, though it is speculative and would benefit from direct pH measurements or additional validation.

result: The study discovered enrichment of nucleoporin proteins (NPP-6/Nup160, NPP-15/Nup133) specifically in lipl-4 Tg lysosome-enriched proteome. Imaging revealed perinuclear clustering of lysosomes in lipl-4 Tg but not daf-2(lf) worms. RNAi knockdown of npp-6 suppressed lipl-4 Tg longevity but not daf-2(lf) or isp-1(lf) longevity. Knockdown of importin-α (ima-3) but not exportin-1 (xpo-1) also suppressed lipl-4 Tg longevity, suggesting nuclear import is required.
evaluation: Claims C121-C133 are well-supported by proteomic data (C121-C123, Figure 6A-B), quantitative imaging analysis (C125-C127, Figures 6C-F), and functional validation through lifespan assays (C128-C132, Figures 6G-J). The specificity of the phenotype to lipl-4 Tg and the requirement for nuclear import machinery provide strong evidence for a lysosome-nucleus signaling axis in this longevity mechanism.

result: The study generated CTNS-1 Lyso-Tag strains and identified 293 lysosome-enriched proteins, with 95 shared with LMP-1 Lyso-IP. CTNS-1 Lyso-IP showed higher enrichment of Ragulator complex (LMTR-2/3/5), mTORC1 regulators (SLC38A9, TRPML1), autophagy proteins, and lysosomal hydrolases compared to LMP-1 Lyso-IP. Imaging confirmed LMTR-3 shows complete overlap with CTNS-1 but only partial overlap with LMP-1, suggesting Ragulator preferentially associates with mature (CTNS-1-positive) lysosomes.
evaluation: Claims C134-C151 are well-supported by proteomic data (Figures 7B-E,G) and validated by imaging (C146-C147, Figure 7F). The differential enrichment of Ragulator and mTORC1 regulators on CTNS-1 vs LMP-1 lysosomes (C145) provides novel insight into lysosomal heterogeneity. The conclusion about Ragulator preference for mature lysosomes is well-supported by both proteomic and imaging data.

result: From screening 95 shared lysosome-enriched proteins, the study identified 5 genes affecting lysosomal function, including v-ATPase subunits (UNC-32, VHA-5), amino acid transporter (SLC-36.2), and novel transmembrane protein R144.6/TMEM144. UNC-32/VHA-5 knockdown decreased lysosome number and increased size. R144.6 knockdown increased lysosomal pH without affecting number/size. R144.6 showed hypodermis-specific lysosomal localization, validated by CRISPR knock-in imaging and tissue-specific Lyso-IP.
evaluation: Claims C152-C165 are supported by functional RNAi screen data (Figures 8A-H), structural prediction (C159, Figure 8I), and validation by imaging and tissue-specific proteomics (C160-C164, Figure 8J). The characterization of R144.6 as a novel hypodermis-specific lysosomal protein demonstrates the power of the Lyso-IP approach for discovering functionally important proteins. The pH measurements using fluorescence lifetime microscopy provide quantitative validation.

result: The presence of LMP-1 and CTNS-1 Lyso-Tag transgenes does not affect worms' developmental timing or lifespan.
evaluation: Claims C44-C45 are supported by developmental timing and lifespan data (Figure 1—supplement 1A-B). This is an important control demonstrating that the transgenic tags do not perturb normal physiology, validating the use of these strains for studying endogenous lysosomal biology.

result: The introduction provides established knowledge about lysosomal function, including their role in metabolism and signaling (C1-C3), protein composition (C11-C23), disease associations (C24-C27), and links to longevity (C28-C32). It also reviews prior methods for lysosomal isolation (C33-C35).
evaluation: Claims C1-C35 represent background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These claims establish the scientific context and rationale for the study but do not represent novel findings from the current work.

result: The study notes that while AAK-2 mediates daf-2(lf) longevity (prior work), this regulation might not involve lysosomal AMPK activation since AAK-2 was not enriched in daf-2(lf) lysosomes. The spatial specificity of AMPK activation may be linked to different longevity mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C112-C114 appropriately integrate prior findings (C112) with current proteomic data (C113) to propose a mechanistic distinction (C114). The inference that daf-2(lf) longevity involves non-lysosomal AMPK is reasonable given the absence of lysosomal AAK-2 enrichment, though this remains speculative without direct functional validation.

result: Prior literature establishes that perinuclear lysosomes are more acidic than peripheral lysosomes, and that lysosomal positioning responds to nutrient signals and metabolic status.
evaluation: Claims C119-C120, C176 represent established knowledge from prior literature (citations provided) that provides context for interpreting the perinuclear clustering observed in lipl-4 Tg worms. These are appropriately cited background claims.

result: The study speculates that increased perinuclear lysosomes in lipl-4 Tg may be associated with increased mature lysosomes (supported by v-ATPase enrichment) and could facilitate transport of proteins/metabolites from lysosomes to nucleus through nuclear pores.
evaluation: Claims C177-C178 are speculative interpretations linking multiple observations (perinuclear clustering, v-ATPase enrichment, nucleoporin enrichment). While the speculation is reasonable and supported by circumstantial evidence, direct demonstration of increased lysosome-nucleus contact or transport would be needed to confirm these hypotheses. The authors appropriately present these as speculative interpretations.

result: Nuclear proteins detected in daf-2(lf) Lyso-IP are mainly involved in RNA splicing. The study speculates this may reflect nucleophagy rather than changes in lysosomal positioning, based on prior yeast literature linking pre-mRNA processing defects to nucleophagy.
evaluation: Claims C179-C181 present a speculative interpretation of nuclear protein enrichment in daf-2(lf) based on functional annotation and analogy to yeast. The speculation is reasonable but lacks direct evidence for nucleophagy in C. elegans daf-2(lf). The absence of perinuclear clustering in daf-2(lf) (C127) supports the distinction from lipl-4 Tg, but the nucleophagy hypothesis requires validation.

result: The study found Ragulator complex shows higher enrichment on CTNS-1 vs LMP-1 lysosomes, confirmed by imaging. This suggests Ragulator preferentially associates with mature lysosomes, which could determine mTORC1/AMPK activation preference. Alternatively, Ragulator may prefer CTNS-1/Cystinosin-containing lysosomes, linking cysteine metabolism to mTORC1 signaling. Prior work shows Cystinosin co-IPs with Ragulator in mammalian cells and antagonizes mTORC1 in Drosophila.
evaluation: Claims C182-C188 integrate current findings (C183-C184) with prior literature (C187-C188) to propose two alternative interpretations (C185-C186). The proteomic and imaging data strongly support differential Ragulator enrichment. The mechanistic interpretations are speculative but well-grounded in the data and prior literature. The authors appropriately present both possibilities without overinterpreting.

result: In lipl-4 Tg worms, Ragulator enrichment is increased with LMP-1 Lyso-IP, possibly due to increased mature lysosomes or induced CTNS-1/Cystinosin levels. CTNS-1 and cysteine cathepsins are increased in lipl-4 Tg. Prior work shows lipl-4 Tg increases β-oxidation, decreases triglycerides, and induces autophagy—phenotypes matching Drosophila Cystinosin overexpression. The study speculates Cystinosin induction might reduce lysosomal mTORC1 signaling in lipl-4 Tg.
evaluation: Claims C189-C196 integrate current proteomic findings (C189, C192) with prior work (C193-C195) to propose a mechanistic link (C196). The proteomic data supporting increased Ragulator and CTNS-1 in lipl-4 Tg is solid (Figure 7G). The speculation about mTORC1 inhibition (C196) is reasonable given the Drosophila data but remains to be directly tested. The alternative explanations (C190-C191) are appropriately presented as possibilities.

result: The study reveals lysosomal AMPK enrichment in lipl-4 Tg and its requirement for longevity, but lysosomal mTORC1/AMPK signaling was not identified in daf-2(lf), isp-1(lf), or glp-1(lf) mutants.
evaluation: Claims C197-C198 summarize key findings about differential involvement of lysosomal AMPK across longevity models. C197 is well-supported by proteomic and lifespan data (Figures 5B-C). C198 is supported by the absence of AMPK/Ragulator enrichment in other models (Figure 5A-B). This highlights mechanism-specific lysosomal remodeling.

result: The study reveals lysosomal protein composition heterogeneity associated with lysosomal status, tissue specificity, and longevity. It confirmed autophagy induction across longevity pathways, unveiled lysosome-nucleus interaction in lipl-4-induced longevity, and underlined spatial control of AMPK activation. The work provides methods and resources for future studies of lysosomal proteome dynamics.
evaluation: Claims C166-C171 represent summary statements of the study's main contributions. These are well-supported by the collective evidence from the results. The claims appropriately distinguish between confirmed findings (autophagy induction, C167), novel discoveries (lysosome-nucleus interaction, C168; AMPK spatial control, C169), and methodological contributions (C170-C171).

result: Proteomic studies can reveal changes in lysosome-organelle interactions. Nuclear proteins were detected in lipl-4 Tg and daf-2(lf) Lyso-IP but not WT, with significantly higher percentage increase in lipl-4 Tg (p<0.05).
evaluation: Claims C172-C175 are supported by proteomic data (Figure 6A, Figure 6—supplement 1I) with appropriate statistical analysis. C172 is a general methodological statement supported by the specific findings. The detection of nuclear proteins in long-lived models (C173-C175) led to the discovery of perinuclear clustering and nucleoporin involvement in longevity.

result: The pull-down efficiency was very low in long-lived worms crossed with CTNS-1 lysoTg, preventing identification of proteins unique to CTNS-1 Lyso-IP in those conditions.
evaluation: Claim C139 describes a technical limitation that prevented complete analysis of CTNS-1 Lyso-IP in longevity models. This is an honest reporting of experimental limitations and explains why certain comparisons could not be made. The authors appropriately acknowledge this constraint.
